assertions_contracts.best_practice: Matches the Go team's own guidance (specification and Effective Go, both cited by the guide): panic is for truly exceptional internal failure, errors are the ordinary mechanism. Nothing in Go 1.26/1.27 changed this.
assertions_contracts.evidence: Fresh full read: guide Sec.4 text is unchanged from run 1 and uncontradicted by the freshly fetched 1.27 announcement or release history.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: No assertion statement in Go: explicit invariant checks in code and tests; panic reserved for broken programmer contracts or irrecoverable internal state; never panic on malformed external data; no recover to fake success; compile-time interface checks do not validate external data.

bounded_work.best_practice: No official Go source prescribes application budgets and nothing contradicts bounded admission; Go 1.27's size-specialized allocation lowers allocation cost but bounds nothing for the application.
bounded_work.evidence: Freshly fetched Go 1.27 announcement confirms the allocation change and contains no position against explicit budgets; Tiger policy stricter than mainstream by design is not a contradiction.
bounded_work.guide_position: Named Max constants for input bytes, items, nesting depth, workers, queue entries, retries and output capture; no goroutine per unbounded input item (bounded workers with admission); no unbounded io.ReadAll (limited reader plus max+1 check); retries need idempotence, shared deadline, bounded backoff.

concurrency.best_practice: The ownership discipline holds, but Go 1.27 made the goroutineleak profile in runtime/pprof generally available - the official, GC-based detector for permanently blocked goroutines - which is the standard tool for the exact leak failure class the guide polices purely by construction discipline.
concurrency.evidence: Freshly fetched Go 1.27 announcement lists the goroutineleak profile as generally available. Fresh text check: the guide never mentions goroutineleak or the pprof leak profile (grep: 0 occurrences), and the run-1 proposal was not applied (FINDINGS pass-2 'What remains open'), so the verdict stands.
concurrency.guide_position: Contexts signal cancellation but do not kill goroutines; every worker has a shutdown path and an owner that waits; sender closes owned channels exactly once; one owner for shared state or a mutex/atomic protocol; happens-before via mutexes/channels/atomics; race detector noted as not a proof.

error_handling.best_practice: Fully aligned with official Go practice (errors are values, wrap for Is/As). Go 1.27 reinforces the 'never compare message strings' rule in practice: encoding/json is now backed by the v2 implementation, so the exact text of some errors can differ even where behaviour is preserved.
error_handling.evidence: Freshly fetched Go 1.27 announcement lists encoding/json/v2 in the standard library and the v2 backing of encoding/json; guide Sec.7 text is unchanged and already states the string-comparison ban the change vindicates.
error_handling.guide_position: Return (value, error) consistently; wrap with %w for errors.Is/As; never compare message strings; handle Close errors; a typed nil in an error interface is not nil; never panic on malformed external data.

formatting.best_practice: Unchanged through 1.27: gofmt output is canonical, and go fix (with new modernizers in 1.27) is the sanctioned mechanical-upgrade path, complementary to - not a replacement for - gofmt.
formatting.evidence: Freshly fetched Go 1.27 announcement lists the new go fix modernizers and nothing altering gofmt's authority; guide Sec.23 and SKILL pairing text are unchanged.
formatting.guide_position: gofmt is authoritative including its tabs; never force spaces or a hard 100-column wrap onto gofmt output; keep lines readable through function design; one reviewed import organizer (goimports in the skill pairing).

memory_ownership.best_practice: Guidance remains correct; Go 1.27's size-specialized allocation (cheaper small allocations) is a runtime improvement and does not revise slice-aliasing or sync.Pool semantics.
memory_ownership.evidence: Freshly fetched Go 1.27 announcement describes the allocation improvement; guide Sec.15 text is unchanged and uncontradicted by it.
memory_ownership.guide_position: GC does not bound queues or prevent leaks; cap workers/channels/maps/bodies/pools; a small subslice can retain a large backing array (clone a small retained result); sync.Pool is a reuse optimization, not storage or a capacity guarantee; check sizes before make.

security.best_practice: Core guidance holds: the os.Root traversal-resistant APIs the guide recommends remain current, and guide Sec.19 correctly notes os.Root is not a sandbox for device files, /proc or mount boundaries. The dependency-vulnerability half of security is scored under static_analysis (the govulncheck gap), as in run 1.
security.evidence: Fresh text check: Sec.19 still bases traversal policy on os.OpenRoot with the not-a-sandbox caveat, and Sec.2 (as remediated) correctly frames 1.24 as the API-availability floor for those APIs, not a support claim.
security.guide_position: Treat unsafe, cgo, reflection, plugins and build directives as trust boundaries; bound HTTP headers/bodies, set timeouts, verify TLS; no pprof/debug endpoints on untrusted interfaces; SSRF care; os.OpenRoot descriptor-relative traversal policy instead of prefix checks; secrets out of errors/logs.

static_analysis.best_practice: The official gate is wider than the guide's: govulncheck (the Go team's vulnerability scanner, golang.org/x/vuln) uses static analysis to report only vulnerabilities that could affect the program, against the Go vulnerability database, and is the standard CI security gate for Go modules.
static_analysis.evidence: govulncheck's official package documentation was freshly fetched: it describes source/binary analysis narrowed to vulnerabilities that could affect the application. Fresh text check: the guide's validation recipe (Sec.27: vet, test, test -race, bench) still never runs it, and the run-1 proposal was not applied, so the verdict stands.
static_analysis.guide_position: go vet in the validation recipe; review go.mod/go.sum, replacements and toolchain directives; checksums verify content, not suitability; audit go generate; no vulnerability-database scan is prescribed anywhere.

testing.best_practice: testing/synctest graduated from experiment to general availability in Go 1.25: tests run in a bubble with a fake clock, making timeout/cancellation tests deterministic without sleeps - the goal the guide prescribes (Sec.28) without naming the tool; Go 1.27 builds on it (for example httptest's synctest-friendly fake network server).
testing.evidence: The Go team's synctest post was freshly fetched and states the graduation to general availability in Go 1.25. Fresh text check: the guide never mentions synctest (grep: 0 occurrences) and the run-1 proposal was not applied, so the verdict stands.
testing.guide_position: Table-driven boundary tests and fuzz targets for parsers; cancellation before/during work, full queues, closed channels, blocked peers, partial I/O, shutdown joins; race tests on concurrent paths; 'do not depend on sleeps: use synchronization or a controlled clock'.

toolchain_pins.best_practice: Go's release policy supports each major release only until two newer majors exist. Go 1.27.0 shipped 2026-08-19 and 1.27.2 on 2026-10-08, so the only supported majors are 1.27 and 1.26; a baseline naming any older major as primary is unsupported.

The run-1 stale verdict is therefore closed. Release history freshly fetched confirms 1.27.2 (2026-10-08) is the latest patch and the two-newer-releases policy.
toolchain_pins.guide_position: Header: 'Primary target: Go 1.27+ (1.26 supported)'; Sec.2: Go 1.24 is an API-availability floor for the os.Root APIs, explicitly not a support claim; GOTOOLCHAIN=local guidance for CI; module/toolchain versions recorded explicitly.
